en: Puggalapaññatti Matrix 4.
Exposition of the Tetads
There are four types of persons:
the person who is not a true man, one who is even less of a true man than that; the person who is a true man, and one who is even more of a true man than that.
The evil person, one who is even more evil than that; the good person, and one who is even better than that.
One of evil nature, one who is even more evil-natured than a person of evil nature; one of beautiful nature, one who is even more beautiful-natured than a person of beautiful nature.
One who is blameworthy, one who abounds in blame; one who has little blame, one who is blameless.
One who gains knowledge by a condensed statement, one who gains knowledge by detailed exposition; one who is guidable, one for whom the words are the limit.

One who possesses relevant eloquence but not spontaneous eloquence; one who possesses spontaneous eloquence but not relevant eloquence; one who possesses both relevant and spontaneous eloquence; and one who possesses neither relevant nor spontaneous eloquence.
These are the four types of persons who discourse on the Dhamma.
There are also four types of persons comparable to clouds.
Four types of persons comparable to mice;
four types of persons comparable to mangoes;
four types of persons comparable to jars.
Four types of persons comparable to water-pools;
four types of persons comparable to oxen;
four types of persons comparable to venomous snakes.
There is a certain person who, without investigating and without scrutinizing, speaks in praise of one who deserves dispraise;
there is a certain person who, without investigating and without scrutinizing, speaks in dispraise of one who deserves praise;
there is a certain person who, without investigating and without scrutinizing, conceives confidence in a matter that inspires lack of confidence. There is a certain person...
There is a person who, without investigating or scrutinizing, conceives lack of confidence toward a matter that merits confidence.
There is a certain person who, having investigated and scrutinized, speaks dispraise of one who deserves dispraise;
there is a certain person who, having investigated and scrutinized, speaks praise of one who deserves praise; there is a certain person...
Having investigated and scrutinized, there is a certain person who conceives lack of confidence in a matter that merits lack of confidence;
and there is a certain person who, having investigated and scrutinized, conceives confidence in a matter that merits confidence.

There is a certain person who speaks dispraise of one deserving of dispraise—truthfully, accurately, and at the proper time—but does not speak praise of one deserving of praise—truthfully, accurately, and at the proper time.

There is a certain person who speaks praise of one worthy of praise—truthfully, accurately, and at the proper time—but does not speak dispraise of one worthy of dispraise—truthfully, accurately, and at the proper time.

There is a certain person who speaks dispraise of one worthy of dispraise—truthfully, accurately, and at the proper time—and also speaks praise of one worthy of praise—truthfully, accurately, and at the proper time. There is a certain person who neither...
One speaks dispraise of one who deserves dispraise—truthfully, accurately, and at the proper time—but does not speak praise of one who deserves praise—truthfully, accurately, and at the proper time.

One lives off the fruits of exertion but not off the fruits of merit; one lives off the fruits of merit but not off the fruits of exertion; one lives off both the fruits of exertion and the fruits of merit; and one lives off neither the fruits of exertion nor the fruits of merit.
One who is in darkness and destined for darkness; one who is in darkness and destined for light; one who is in light and destined for darkness; one who is in light and destined for light.
One who is bent down and bent down; one who is bent down and raised up; one who is raised up and bent down; one who is raised up and raised up.
These are the four types of persons compared to trees.
One who places standard on form and has faith in form; one who places standard on sound and has faith in sound;
one who places standard on the coarse and has faith in the coarse; one who places standard on the Dhamma and has faith in the Dhamma.
There is a certain person who practices for his own benefit, but not for the benefit of others.
There is a certain person who practices for the benefit of others, but not for his own benefit;
there is a certain person who practices both for his own benefit and for the benefit of others;
and there is a certain person who practices neither for his own benefit nor for the benefit of others.
There is a certain person who torments himself and is devoted to the practice of self-tormenting;
there is a certain person who torments others and is devoted to the practice of tormenting others;
there is a certain person who both torments himself and is devoted to the practice of self-tormenting, and also torments others and is devoted to the practice of tormenting others.

There is a certain person who neither torments himself nor is devoted to the practice of self-torment, and neither torments others nor is devoted to the practice of tormenting others. Being neither a torturer of self nor a torturer of others,
he dwells in this very life free from craving, extinguished, cooled, experiencing bliss, having become one with the Brahma-state—
yet he is still possessed of lust, hatred, and delusion.
There is a certain person who attains internal mental serenity but does not attain higher wisdom and insight into phenomena;
there is a certain person who attains higher wisdom and insight into phenomena but does not attain internal mental serenity;
and there is a certain person who attains both internal mental serenity and higher wisdom and insight into phenomena.
There is a certain person who is neither an attainer of internal mental tranquility nor an attainer of higher wisdom through insight into phenomena.

There is the person who goes with the stream; the person who goes against the stream; the person who is established in himself; and the person who has crossed over, gone to the further shore, and stands on dry land—the brahmin.

There is the one of little learning who is not perfected by what he has heard; the one of little learning who is perfected by what he has heard; the one of great learning who is not perfected by what he has heard; and the one of great learning who is perfected by what he has heard.
The ascetic Macala, the ascetic Paduma, the ascetic Puṇḍarīka, and the ascetic Sukhumāla among ascetics.
This is the tetrad.
